items.readable_text:
Content:
The cumulative distribution function (or CDF) of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is a function [MATH: F(x)] such that

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

Content:
Similar to a probability distribution function, a cumulative distribution function is another method that we can use to describe the distribution of a random variable.

Content:
To illustrate the usage of a cumulative distribution function in a concrete situation, suppose that the random variable [MATH: X] represents the roll of a fair six-sided die. Then

Content:
- The probability of rolling a number less than or equal to [MATH: 2] (i.e., rolling a [MATH: 1] or a [MATH: 2]) is
[MATH: P(X \leq 2) = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}.]
So, we write [MATH: F(2) = \dfrac{1}{3}.]
- The probability of rolling a number less than or equal to [MATH: 5] (i.e. rolling a [MATH: 1,] [MATH: 2,] [MATH: 3,] [MATH: 4,] or [MATH: 5]) is
[MATH: P(X \leq 5) = \dfrac{5}{6}.]
So, we write [MATH: F(5) = \dfrac{5}{6}.]

Content:
One benefit to using a cumulative distribution function is that it allows us to easily compute the probability of a random variable over an interval. In general, we have the following rule:

Content:
[MATH: P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)]

Content:
Continuing the example above, if we want to calculate the probability that the roll of the six-sided die is greater than [MATH: 2] and less than or equal to [MATH: 5,] then we can use the rule as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P(2 < X ≤ 5)|= F(5) − F(2); = (5)/(6) − (1)/(3); = (5)/(6) − (2)/(6); = (3)/(6); = (1)/(2)]

Content:
Indeed, the result is correct. The only numbers greater than [MATH: 2] and less than or equal to [MATH: 5] are [MATH: 3,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 5,] and the probability of rolling any of these three numbers is [MATH: \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is the function [MATH: F(x)] defined by

[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

So, we have

[MATH: F(5)|= P(X ≤ 5); = P(X ∈ {1, 3, 5}); = P(X = 1) + P(X = 3) + P(X = 5); = P(X ∈ {1, 3}) + P(X = 5); = P(X ≤ 3) + P(X = 5); = F(3) + P(X = 5).]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X = 5)|= F(5) − F(3); = 0.50 − 0.45; = 0.05.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: Y] is the function [MATH: F(y)] defined by

[MATH: F(y) = P(Y \leq y).]

To compute the probability of a random variable [MATH: Y] over an interval, we can use the rule

[MATH: P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a).]

Here, we want to compute [MATH: P\left( 2 \leq Y < 5 \right).] However, this interval is stated in the form [MATH: a \leq Y < b,] not [MATH: a < Y \leq b.]

So first, we must convert the interval [MATH: 2 \leq Y < 5] to the form [MATH: a < X \leq b.] Looking at the given possible values of [MATH: Y,] we see that [MATH: 2 \leq Y] is equivalent to [MATH: 1 < Y,] and [MATH: Y< 5] is equivalent to [MATH: Y \leq 4.] Therefore,

[MATH: P(2 ≤ Y < 5)|= P(1 < Y ≤ 4); = F(4) − F(1); = (3)/(4) − (1)/(4); = (1)/(2).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The cumulative distribution function (or CDF) of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is a function [MATH: F(x)] such that

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

Content:
Similar to a probability distribution function, a cumulative distribution function is another method that we can use to describe the distribution of a random variable.

Content:
To illustrate the usage of a cumulative distribution function in a concrete situation, suppose that the random variable [MATH: X] represents the roll of a fair six-sided die. Then

Content:
- The probability of rolling a number less than or equal to [MATH: 2] (i.e., rolling a [MATH: 1] or a [MATH: 2]) is
[MATH: P(X \leq 2) = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}.]
So, we write [MATH: F(2) = \dfrac{1}{3}.]
- The probability of rolling a number less than or equal to [MATH: 5] (i.e. rolling a [MATH: 1,] [MATH: 2,] [MATH: 3,] [MATH: 4,] or [MATH: 5]) is
[MATH: P(X \leq 5) = \dfrac{5}{6}.]
So, we write [MATH: F(5) = \dfrac{5}{6}.]

Content:
One benefit to using a cumulative distribution function is that it allows us to easily compute the probability of a random variable over an interval. In general, we have the following rule:

Content:
[MATH: P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)]

Content:
Continuing the example above, if we want to calculate the probability that the roll of the six-sided die is greater than [MATH: 2] and less than or equal to [MATH: 5,] then we can use the rule as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P(2 < X ≤ 5)|= F(5) − F(2); = (5)/(6) − (1)/(3); = (5)/(6) − (2)/(6); = (3)/(6); = (1)/(2)]

Content:
Indeed, the result is correct. The only numbers greater than [MATH: 2] and less than or equal to [MATH: 5] are [MATH: 3,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 5,] and the probability of rolling any of these three numbers is [MATH: \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing a CDF Given the PMF

Example Prompt:
Given that the discrete random variable [MATH: Y] has the probability mass function [MATH: f(y),] shown in the table below, and the cumulative distribution function [MATH: F(y),] compute [MATH: F(2).]

| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| [MATH: f(y)] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{8}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{8}] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: Y] is the function [MATH: F(y)] defined by

[MATH: F(y) = P(Y \leq y).]

So, we have
[MATH: F(2)|= P(Y ≤ 2); = P(Y ∈ {1, 2}); = P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2); = f(1) + f(2); = (1)/(2) + (1)/(8); = (5)/(8).]

---

Item 5 — Example: Computing the Probability of an Event Given the CDF

Example Prompt:
Given that the discrete random variable [MATH: X] has the cumulative distribution function [MATH: F(x)] shown in the table below, compute [MATH: P(X=5).]

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 7] | [MATH: 9] |
| [MATH: F(x)] | [MATH: 0.15] | [MATH: 0.45] | [MATH: 0.50] | [MATH: 0.90] | [MATH: 1.0] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: X] is the function [MATH: F(x)] defined by

[MATH: F(x) = P(X \leq x).]

So, we have

[MATH: F(5)|= P(X ≤ 5); = P(X ∈ {1, 3, 5}); = P(X = 1) + P(X = 3) + P(X = 5); = P(X ∈ {1, 3}) + P(X = 5); = P(X ≤ 3) + P(X = 5); = F(3) + P(X = 5).]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X = 5)|= F(5) − F(3); = 0.50 − 0.45; = 0.05.]

Item 8 — Example: Computing a Probability Over an Interval Given the CDF

Example Prompt:
Given that the discrete random variable [MATH: Y] has the cumulative distribution function [MATH: F(y)] shown in the table below, compute [MATH: P\left( 2 \leq Y < 5 \right).]

| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: F(y)] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] | [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}] | [MATH: \dfrac{3}{4}] | [MATH: \dfrac{5}{6}] | [MATH: 1] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable [MATH: Y] is the function [MATH: F(y)] defined by

[MATH: F(y) = P(Y \leq y).]

To compute the probability of a random variable [MATH: Y] over an interval, we can use the rule

[MATH: P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a).]

Here, we want to compute [MATH: P\left( 2 \leq Y < 5 \right).] However, this interval is stated in the form [MATH: a \leq Y < b,] not [MATH: a < Y \leq b.]

So first, we must convert the interval [MATH: 2 \leq Y < 5] to the form [MATH: a < X \leq b.] Looking at the given possible values of [MATH: Y,] we see that [MATH: 2 \leq Y] is equivalent to [MATH: 1 < Y,] and [MATH: Y< 5] is equivalent to [MATH: Y \leq 4.] Therefore,

[MATH: P(2 ≤ Y < 5)|= P(1 < Y ≤ 4); = F(4) − F(1); = (3)/(4) − (1)/(4); = (1)/(2).]

[MATH: P(X \leq x) = F(x)]

[MATH: P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a).]
